title: The Lund Oat Drink That a Dairy Manager Spat Out
dek: In 1994 two Lund University researchers set up a company around a patented oat drink that much of the food industry thought nobody would buy.

story.event: Taking a patented oat drink out of a Lund University laboratory and founding Ceba
story.summary: In the early 1990s Lund University food chemist Rickard Öste and doctoral student Angeliki Triantafyllou developed an enzyme process that turned oats into a milk-like drink, in a project begun with the Swedish Farmers' Association; the process was patented in 1993 and in 1994 they founded Cereal Base Ceba AB, the predecessor of Oatly. Parts of the industry dismissed the drink, including, by Öste's account, Arla's marketing manager, and early partnerships failed before oat farmers invested so it could be sold under the Oatly name.
paragraphs: At a conference in Japan in 1985, Rickard Öste, a food chemist from Lund University, noticed that a coin in a vending machine would buy a carton of soy milk with a long shelf life. His department had studied lactose intolerance for two decades, and his own attempts to strip lactose from milk kept costing protein quality. The machine set him wondering whether a milk-like drink could be made from something else.

Soy seemed wrong, since some people are allergic to soy and other legumes. Barley milk did not taste nice; nor did rye. Oats, a staple Swedish crop, came next. In the early 1990s the work became a collaboration with the Swedish Farmers' Association, which wanted better uses for oat by-products usually sold as animal feed. Angeliki Triantafyllou, a doctoral student in biotechnology, joined and became a driving force behind the enzyme process that turned oats and water into a drink. It was patented in 1993.

Öste had seen, as a visiting researcher near San Francisco, how Silicon Valley carried research into the market, and he wanted to do the same without leaving his university work. In 1994 he and Triantafyllou founded Cereal Base Ceba AB; he kept his post at Lund and became Ceba's chief executive in 1996. The reception was cold. Early batches were made on modified soy milk equipment, and some in the industry called the drink "undrinkable". Once the patent was secured, Öste later recalled, he invited Arla's marketing manager to taste it. The man took a sip, spat it out and said, "You'll never sell this." Without patents, Triantafyllou said later, the firm "would have stood no chance against the large multinational food companies".

Partnerships came and went. A creamy diet soup with a Swedish food company did not sell, an oat drink in Britain found only lukewarm interest, and a venture on oat yoghurt with Danone failed. Öste decided he needed to own the product, and Swedish oat farmers, looking for new outlets for their crop, invested so it could reach shops under the Oatly name. Two decades on, the oat drink from Skåne was sold around the world and Arla counted it as a competitor.

quote.text: There never was, there never will be, nor is there now, a man who is always blamed, or a man who is always praised.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: The dairy manager's verdict and the acclaim that came years later were both real, and neither was final. The verse suggests that a drink spat out one year and praised the next had changed less than the verdicts on it.

reflection: It is worth noticing who did the tasting. The man who spat out the oat drink worked for Arla, a dairy business with its own reasons not to like it. His reaction was real information, but it said something about him as well as about the drink.

You will get verdicts on your work too, some flattering and some harsh, and on a tired day either can feel final. The Dhammapada's plain point is that nobody is only blamed or only praised. Öste also kept his university post for years while the company found its feet. A slow start on two tracks is still a start.
invitation: Think of one recent harsh reaction to something you made. Write down who gave it and what they had at stake, then decide whether it should change anything you do this week.

cross_checks.claim: Öste's oat drink research at Lund grew out of work on lactose intolerance.
In 1994 Öste founded Ceba AB, the predecessor and parent of Oatly, with Triantafyllou as co-founder.
The research began at Lund in the early 1990s and aimed to raise the value of oat by-products sold as animal feed.
Parts of the food industry rejected the early drink.
Early partnerships failed and Swedish oat farmers invested so the drink could be sold as Oatly.

research_notes: Founders: the slate named only Rickard Öste. The European Patent Office (2026) says Öste and Angeliki Triantafyllou co-founded Cereal Base Ceba AB in 1994; Öste's own CV calls him founder and major owner of Ceba; Wikipedia says he co-founded Oatly with his brother Björn in 1994, but Lund University's alumni article says Björn joined in 1997 after selling his IT security business. The story credits Öste and Triantafyllou with founding Ceba and does not name Björn, to stay inside the word limit. Dates: the Lund article puts Öste's interest in the 1980s (the 1985 Japan conference); the EPO puts the research in the early 1990s and the patent in 1993; Time (2018) says Oatly was founded about 25 years earlier. The Arla tasting rests only on Öste's own account in the Lund article and is attributed to him; the EPO separately reports that some in the industry called the drink 'undrinkable'. The order of early partnerships is not dated in the sources: the 2016 article by Read and Wiltbank lists the soup, a UK oat drink (which it calls 'Mill Milk') and the Danone yoghurt, then the farmers' investment; the Lund article mentions ICA selling it as Solhavre and the first commercial product in British supermarkets just before 2000. The story keeps these as a loose sequence without dates and leaves out ICA. Triantafyllou's patent quotation appears in two English wordings (EPO finalist page and a vegconomist report); the EPO wording is used. The Lund article's 2021 turnover figure (6 billion kronor) is not used. Funding is marked mixed: university and farmers' association research, then farmer investment and later Björn Öste's money. The Dhammapada verse is applied by analogy.
